title: Slide 1 · Trustworthy ML: Uncertainty, Robustness, and Interpretability
question: If a cart planner raises its assumed success chance from 0.5 to 0.8, has the crossing itself become easier?
answer: Only the estimate changed. Independent observations under comparable conditions are needed to tell whether crossing success changed.

title: Slide 2 · Keep the forecast separate from the result
question: Does one failure on a prediction of 0.9 prove that the model is overconfident?
answer: A calibrated 0.9 forecast still allows failures. Check a group of comparable forecasts and report its size.

title: Slide 3 · Read a reliability diagram
question: A bin of 20 predictions averaging 0.3 contains 10 successes. On which side of the diagonal does it fall?
answer: The point is (0.3, 0.5), above the diagonal. These events occurred more often than the forecasts suggested.

title: Slide 4 · Measure error without losing the individual bins
question: If you average the two absolute gaps without the counts, what do you get and why is it different?
answer: The unweighted mean is 0.15. It gives the five-case group just as much influence as the ten-case group.

title: Slide 5 · Separate confidence, accuracy and uncertainty
question: May we fit the new score of 0.6 here and call this group's Brier score an independent evaluation?
answer: This group supplied the replacement value. Estimate calibration parameters on validation examples and evaluate the frozen change on separate cases.

title: Slide 6 · Change one input deliberately
question: Does this test establish that completing one extra set raises an actual exam score by five points?
answer: It measures a change in the model's output after editing a record. It supplies no comparison of actual outcomes under an intervention on practice.

title: Slide 7 · Change the population mix
question: The new overall error is 9 points. Could changing only the mix of these fixed two groups explain it?
answer: A weighted average of 2 and 8 lies between 2 and 8. Check whether a within-group error changed, other groups appeared, or measurements differ.

title: Slide 8 · Ask who experiences the mistakes
question: If three new touch attempts did not need help, does the touch false-negative rate change?
answer: No. Its denominator contains only attempts that needed help. Track false-positive rates as a separate consequence for attempts that did not need help.

title: Slide 9 · Explain the output and state what the test supports
question: How could two differently scaled features make a raw weight comparison misleading?
answer: Hours and minutes describe the same duration. A coefficient of 10 points per hour is 1/6 point per minute. The contribution for a two-hour record stays 20 with either unit.

title: Slide 11 · From this module to the next
question: Why save the split and evaluation rule before comparing your final models?
answer: A fixed split makes the comparison repeatable. Freezing the evaluation rule helps prevent a favorable test outcome from becoming the reason for choosing a model.

title: Office hours · Can a well-calibrated model still be unhelpful?
question: Can a well-calibrated model still be unhelpful?
answer: Yes. If half the attempts succeed, assigning 0.5 to everyone can match the overall frequency while giving no way to distinguish easier attempts from harder ones. Examine discrimination and the actual decisions as well.

title: Office hours · Why do the bin boundaries matter?
question: Why do the bin boundaries matter?
answer: A wide bin can average together overprediction in one subgroup and underprediction in another. Very narrow bins may have just a few outcomes. Report the bin definition and count alongside every estimate.

title: Office hours · When should the system defer a decision?
question: When should the system defer a decision?
answer: A help tool might send uncertain cases for review. Pick the threshold using validation data and the costs of mistakes and review. Report how many cases it covers and how often it errs among both decided and deferred cases.

title: Exercise 1
question: A model gives ten predictions of 0.8 with five observed successes and twenty of 0.5 with ten successes. Locate the overconfident group and compute ECE.
answer: The first group's frequency is 0.5, a 0.3 overprediction. The second group has zero gap. ECE = (10/30) × 0.3 = 0.10.

title: Exercise 2
question: Compare Brier scores when one outcome is 0 and two models assign 0.2 and 0.8.
answer: The scores are 0.04 and 0.64. The 0.2 forecast scores better on this case. Compare many held-out cases to evaluate the models.

title: Exercise 3
question: Set logging drops the last practice set whenever a student uses a phone. Design a paired stress test for the score model.
answer: Take records with at least one set, evaluate original and one-set-lower copies, and compare predictions and absolute errors within each pair. Verify the error exists against independent logs and report counts by input device.

title: Exercise 4
question: An evaluation set is 80% group A with MAE 3 and 20% B with MAE 7. Predict the MAE if the deployment mix becomes 50/50.
answer: The original average is 0.8 × 3 + 0.2 × 7 = 3.8. The new average is 5. Recheck both group-specific errors on fresh deployment examples.

title: Exercise 5
question: A model misses 2 of 4 actual help needs in one group and 2 of 20 in another. What deserves follow-up?
answer: The observed miss rates are 50% and 10%. Investigate label quality, data collection and the decision threshold. The four-case denominator makes the first estimate especially unstable.

title: Exercise 6
question: The model assigns a positive coefficient to extra practice. Can your report recommend extra practice as a proven way to raise scores?
answer: You can explain the model's response to editing practice counts. A causal recommendation requires a design and assumptions that address how practice was chosen and what outcomes would otherwise have occurred.
